text: Wireshark lets you inspect every packet crossing one interface in complete detail, but running that kind of full capture everywhere, all the time, across an entire network would produce more data than any SOC could store or review. NetFlow solves a different problem: instead of recording everything about every packet, it records a small amount of metadata about every traffic flow — one direction, same source and destination IP, port, and protocol.

NetFlow originated at Cisco and now underlies the open IPFIX standard. A flow record is built around the 5-tuple — source IP, destination IP, source port, destination port, protocol — plus packet count, byte count, and duration. A file download between two internal hosts might produce a record reading 5.1 megabytes, 3,812 packets, 41 seconds, over TCP port 445. That's the entire record — no filename, no file contents, nothing from inside the payload at all.

That compactness is the whole point. A router can export thousands of flow records a second without slowing down, and a collector can store months of that metadata in the space full packet capture would burn through in a single busy day. That's why flow monitoring gives a SOC visibility into every conversation happening across an entire network, not just the one link a packet-capture tool happens to be watching.

The tradeoff is direct: NetFlow can tell you that 5.1 megabytes moved between two hosts, but nothing about what was actually inside it. A legitimate backup job and someone quietly exfiltrating a sensitive file can produce nearly identical flow records if the volume and timing happen to line up — flow data alone can't tell those two stories apart.

Flow data is where broad, network-wide visibility starts, not where a deep investigation ends. Next up: deep packet inspection versus flow analysis — the tool that actually looks inside the payload a flow record can only summarize, and why you don't just run it on everything.
